title: The plain month
hookLine: a month with no holidays, when ordinary life is the practice
tomorrow: why light a lamp you're not allowed to use?

lines: LAUNDRY, INBOX, NOTHING ON THE CALENDAR.
cards: The week after a big trip: laundry piled up, inbox full, nothing on the calendar. After a month crowded with holy days comes Cheshvan, a month with none at all.
Some people even call it bitter Cheshvan, for the empty calendar. The rabbis tell a story that answers that. Hillel the Elder is heading out, and his students fall in beside him.
Where are you going, teacher? To do a commandment, he says. Which one?

teach.b: His students stop. A bath is a commandment? Hillel answers with a picture.
Statues of kings stand in the theaters and the circuses, and someone is appointed to scrub and polish them, and is honored for it.
How much more me, he says, created in the image, as it's written: "for in the image of God made He man." Washing his own body was a way of honoring the image. That's Cheshvan's practice.
No shofar, no hut, no candles: just the ordinary day, done with care.
Proverbs puts it in one line: "In all thy ways acknowledge Him." The Talmud asks which short verse the whole Torah hangs on, and one answer is that one. In all your ways, not just on the holy days.
The commute, the dishes, the bath. And notice the human part of Hillel's answer.
The verse he quotes is about every person, not only kings or sages. The same image is in the stranger at the bus stop, the cashier, the kid nobody sits with. So the plain month isn't empty.
It's where you find out whether the holy days came home with you.

how: Cheshvan has no festivals; Jews who keep a daily practice carry on with ordinary prayers, blessings over food and weekly Shabbat, and some use the quiet month to settle a routine begun during the holidays.

o: he'd agree: rest up until the next holiday comes.

games.why: Hillel walked to the bathhouse calling it a commandment. in all thy ways, not just on the holy days.

practice: For the sit, choose one plain thing you'll do today anyway: wash your hands, make your bed, pour a glass of water. Walk through it slowly in your mind, the way Hillel walked to the bathhouse: this too, done with care.
When the moment comes later, do it a little slower than usual.
